Events leading to the outbreak of war in Europe, September 1, 1939:
I. Speculation as to Axis designs, apart from Czechoslovakia, January-March 15, 1939
II. Occupation of Czechoslovakia by Germany, March 15, 1939; refusal of the United States to recognize extinction of the Czechoslovak Republic
III. Tension in Europe following German occupation of Czechoslovakia, March 16–April 14, 1939
IV. President Roosevelt’s messages of April 14 to Germany and Italy requesting reassurance that neither power contemplated military aggression
V. Increasing German pressure on Poland, April 15–August 21, 1939
VI. Anglo-French-Soviet negotiations attempting to reach an agreement against aggression
VII. The improvement of German-Soviet relations culminating in the Treaty of Nonaggression signed at Moscow, August 23, 1939
VIII. Final efforts to preserve peace in Europe; appeals by President Roosevelt to Germany and Italy, August 22–31, 1939

Beginning of European Phase of World War II:
I. Invasion of Poland by Germany and entry of the British and French into the war, September 1–16, 1939
II. Intervention of the Soviet Union in Poland, September 17, 1939, and speculation as to further spread of the war
III. The Boundary and Friendship Treaty between Germany and the Soviet Union signed at Moscow, September 28, 1939, and early attempts at German-Soviet wartime cooperation
IV. Peace movements and proposals following the occupation of Poland
V. Appeals of President Roosevelt to the belligerents against aerial bombardment of civilian populations
VI. Suspension of the London Naval Treaty of March 25, 1936
VII. Establishment of Anglo-French purchasing board in the United States for the coordination of British and French purchasing during the war
VIII. Evacuation of the American Embassy staff from Poland and maintenance of diplomatic contact with the Polish Government; retention of the American Consulate General in Warsaw
IX. Informal representations by the United States to the Rumanian Government to secure the release of ex-President Moscicki of Poland
X. Protection by the United States of interests of belligerent powers

Repatriation of Americans and others from belligerent countries:
I. Emergency measures for the protection and repatriation of American citizens abroad upon the outbreak of war
II. Efforts of the United States to secure the repatriation of civilian enemy aliens in belligerent countries

Neutrality policy of the United States:
I. Revision of United States neutrality legislation
II. Proclamation of United States neutrality upon the outbreak of war; other measures for the preservation of United States neutrality

Control of commerce by belligerent governments:
I. Establishment of control measures by the belligerents interfering with neutral commerce; reservations by the United States of American rights
II. Representations to the allied governments against application of control measures interfering with trade between the United States and neutral countries
III. Representations to the German Government against detention of neutral ships and cargoes destined for the United States

Measures to secure adequate supplies of raw materials:
I. Formulation of plans to acquire adequate stockpiles of strategic raw materials
II. Negotiations with the International Rubber Regulation Committee, through the British and Netherlands Governments, for adequate releases of rubber
III. Negotiations with the International Tin Regulation Committee, through the British and Netherlands Governments, for adequate releases of tin
IV. Arrangements for the wartime operation of the International Sugar Agreement

item.ref: Concern of the United States over Soviet demands on Finland and the outbreak of the Winter War
